Overview Momentum — UX case study

Rebuilding creative Momentum

A platform that helps creatives understand what's blocking them and take one manageable step back toward making.

ProjectPersonal
CategoryProduct Design / UX
ToolsFigma, FigJam
Year2026

01 The problem

When designers get stuck, more inspiration isn't always the answer.

Designers often already have ideas, references and experience — and still struggle to decide what to do next. They open Pinterest, Behance or Instagram looking for clarity and come back with more choices, more comparison and more pressure.

Stuck→Search→More choice→Overthink→Still stuck
Designers need a simple way to recognise what is blocking them and take a manageable next step, instead of getting stuck in more inspiration, comparison or overthinking.

02 The solution

The product does not add more ideas. It helps decide what to do next.

Momentum is a creative recovery platform. It helps designers identify what is blocking them, then guides them to one small, focused activity that gets them back to their work.

05 Research approach

Before designing, I needed to understand the moment of getting stuck.

Quantitative0Survey responses — frequency, triggers and coping across practising and student designers.
Qualitative0In-depth interviews — a specific recent block: what it felt like and what finally moved them.

06 Quantitative findings

The block is common and inspiration is often the first response.

0%experience creative blocks regularly
0%get stuck because of too much inspiration and comparison
0%look for online inspiration first
0%would use or consider a dedicated tool
Creative block is not simply an absence of ideas. Comparison, too much input and uncertainty about where to start were also part of the experience.

Based on 18 survey responses — a small sample, not all designers.

07 Qualitative analysis

Across four interviews, the same pattern kept surfacing.

Designers described a mix of internal doubt and external pressure. What they wanted was not another complicated system — it was a small nudge that helped them begin.

Self-doubt

Designers judge the work before it exists — the idea is rejected in their head first. Mentioned unprompted by 4 / 4 interviewees.

External pressure

Deadlines, client expectation and visible peer work all raise the stakes of starting. Strongest among freelancers.

Overthinking

More possibilities make the decision harder, not easier. Choice becomes the block. Linked to the 50% inspiration finding.

Simple support

Nobody wanted another system to maintain. They wanted a nudge, then to be left alone. Shaped the scope of the product.

08 Competitive landscape

The opportunity was not another place to browse. It was what happens after browsing fails.

PlatformDesign languageWhat worksWhere it falls short
PinterestDense masonry, image-first, near-zero chromeEffortless collecting and board-buildingInfinite feed rewards browsing over finishing
BehanceEditorial project pages, long-form casesDepth — you see the whole processPolished outcomes invite comparison, not action
DribbbleTight square shots, high craft densityFast visual reference for micro-decisionsShots without context set an unreal bar
InstagramSocial feed, algorithmic, creator-ledConstant exposure to new workMixes creative input with social pressure

10 Key insight

The ideas were there. The next step was not.

Designers were not always searching for creativity — they were often struggling with choosing, starting, or knowing when to step away. They had ideas but couldn't choose between them; they knew what they wanted but couldn't start; they had too many references to hold in their head.

Designers don't need more inspiration. They need a clear, manageable next step.

13 Problem statement

Research

72% get blocked regularly. 50% blame too much inspiration and comparison.

Insight

The shortage isn't ideas. It's a decision about what to do in the next five minutes.

Problem

No tool supports the moment of being stuck.

Designers need a simple way to recognise what is blocking them and take a manageable next step, instead of getting stuck in more inspiration, comparison or overthinking.

18 Information architecture

Each journey, mapped as its own flow.

Seven task flows behind the structure — pick one to watch it trace from start to finish.

19 Low fidelity

Before polish, I needed to know whether the structure worked.

Started with low-fidelity screens because they were quick enough to change. The goal was to validate hierarchy, navigation and the recovery flow before visual styling made decisions harder to revisit.

20 Mid fidelity

With the structure working, I removed visual styling so hierarchy had to carry the experience.

The mid-fidelity stage tested answer states, the activity experience, result, collections and saved content without relying on colour or decoration. Swipe through, or use the arrows.

21 Design system

A focused visual system gives the recovery experience one consistent voice.

A dark canvas, one dominant accent and a small set of supporting colours, so the primary action stays visually clear. Tap a colour to read what it does.

23 Components & icons

Components built to be read in a glance.

Buttons — Primary (neon), Secondary (blue), Neutral (white) and Disabled.
Navigation — Home, Collection, Recovery, Articles, Profile.
Exercise card — title, activity type and time at a glance.
Answer states — correct and incorrect feedback, plus a step progress bar.

Icon set — one outline style throughout.

24 Usability testing

The prototype worked and the test showed exactly where the experience could be clearer.

Participants: three freelancers and two in-house designers, 2–6 years in. Moderated, think-aloud, on the clickable prototype.

Tasks tested: understand the check-in · identify the creative block · complete a recovery activity · identify the primary action · return to work.

4/5completed a micro-task and said they were ready to go back to their own canvas
≤8minutes from opening the app to being back in the work, across every completed run
What was observed
Everyone read the detected block as accurate for how they'd been feeling.
Two participants tried to tap the confidence badge, expecting an explanation behind it.
The result screen's two buttons were read correctly as "Try again" and "Back to home".
One participant abandoned the activity.

Small sample: five participants, not statistically representative.

26 Iteration

Two small UI changes removed a lot of unnecessary friction.

BeforeAfter
BeforeAfter

Drag the handle — or use the arrow keys.

Before — Secondary actions competed visually with main CTAs, causing hesitation during task selection.
After — Re-architected hierarchy, promoting the primary action with a solid #CEFE1C fill.

26 Prototype & reflection

The goal was never to maximise screen time. It was to minimise the time between stuck and moving.

Momentum started with a simple observation: creative block is often an action problem, not an information shortage. The final experience turns that insight into a focused loop — recognise the block, take a micro-step, and return to the work.
